title: Sentinel Workspace, Roles, and Content Hub

questions.sub_skill: Create and connect workspaces in Microsoft Sentinel
questions.prompt: Your organisation has 12 subscriptions in one tenant, all in one country, with one SOC. A colleague proposes one workspace per subscription for isolation. The case against?
options: Sentinel supports a maximum of four workspaces per tenant
Every cross-subscription investigation then needs cross-workspace queries, and analytics rules must be duplicated and maintained in each workspace
Workspaces cannot be queried together at all
Costs scale per workspace rather than per gigabyte
questions.explanation: Correlation is easy inside a workspace and awkward across them. The legitimate drivers for multiple workspaces are regulatory, organisational or contractual — none of which apply here.
why_not: The case against is not a workspace limit. It is the cost of correlating and maintaining detections across workspaces.
Workspaces can be queried together. It is awkward, and that awkwardness is the cost the design imposes.
The argument against is operational - awkward cross-workspace correlation and duplicated rules - not a per-workspace price.

questions.prompt: An analyst reports they cannot close an incident. They hold Microsoft Sentinel Reader. Which role do they need, and which would you avoid giving them?
options: Contributor; avoid Responder, which cannot triage
Responder, which adds incident management; avoid Contributor, which would let them edit and delete detection logic
Playbook Operator; avoid Reader, which is redundant
Automation Contributor; avoid Responder, which is for engineers
questions.explanation: Responder is the analyst role: everything Reader can do, plus assigning, reclassifying and closing incidents. Contributor is for the people who write detections. Automation Contributor is assigned to the Sentinel service, not to people.
why_not: Contributor would let them edit and delete detection logic, and Responder can triage - it is the analyst role.
Playbook Operator lists, views and runs playbooks. It does not grant incident management.
Automation Contributor is assigned to the Sentinel service, not to people, and Responder is the analyst role.

questions.prompt: Someone needs to build playbooks. Which permission does that require?
options: Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator
Logic App permissions — playbooks are Logic Apps, and no Sentinel role grants authoring
Microsoft Sentinel Contributor at workspace scope
Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor on the workspace resource group
questions.explanation: Playbook Operator lets someone list, view and manually run playbooks. Creating and editing them is governed by Logic App permissions, because that is what a playbook is.
why_not: Playbook Operator lets someone list, view and manually run playbooks, not create or edit them.
No Sentinel role grants playbook authoring. That is governed by Logic App permissions.
Automation Contributor is for the Sentinel service to run playbooks, not for people authoring them.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and use content hub solutions
questions.prompt: A team installs 40 content hub solutions in an afternoon and reports that Sentinel is deployed. What is missing?
options: Data connectors, which install separately from solutions
Active analytics rules — installing a solution delivers rule templates, and nothing detects anything until you create rules from them
A commitment tier, without which rules cannot run
Workspace manager, which distributes the solutions
questions.explanation: Installing puts templates in the workspace. A tenant with forty solutions installed and no active rules has a full catalogue and no detections. Creating a rule from a template is also where you tune the threshold rather than accepting it.
why_not: Even with data flowing, templates detect nothing. Rules have to be created from them.
Analytics rules do not depend on a commitment tier. What is missing is the rules themselves.
Workspace manager distributes content across workspaces. It is not needed to activate detections in one.

questions.sub_skill: Create and connect workspaces in Microsoft Sentinel
questions.prompt: You set a commitment tier too high in week one. What can you do about it, and when?
options: Reduce it immediately; commitment tiers are evaluated daily
You can increase at any time — which restarts the 31-day commitment period — but to decrease or return to pay-as-you-go you must wait out the 31 days
Nothing; commitment tiers are fixed for 12 months
Switch to pay-as-you-go immediately, then re-commit at the lower tier
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is the point: increases are easy and restart the clock, decreases wait. Commit cautiously on guessed volume, especially in a new deployment.
why_not: A commitment tier cannot be reduced immediately. Decreases wait out the 31-day commitment period.
The commitment period is 31 days, not 12 months.
Returning to pay-as-you-go is also a decrease, so it waits out the 31 days as well.
